questions.question: Identify the component of the TICLS framework which assesses a / child’s muscle tone and spontaneous movement? a). Tone b). Interactiveness c). Look/Gaze d). Speech/Cry
questions.solution_html:
• a) Tone
  • Height/Length (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  Length is measured in children below 2 years using an infantometer, with the child
  • lying down (known as recumbent or crown-heel length).
  •  The child’s head is placed against the fixed headpiece, the body is kept straight, and
  • the knees and ankles are gently pressed flat against the board.
  •  Standing height (stature) is measured in children aged 2 years and above using a
  • stadiometer or wall-mounted measuring board, with bare feet and the child standing
  • erect.
  •  The head is positioned horizontally, and the measurement is recorded to the nearest
  • 0.1 cm.
  • Left Heart Obstructive Lesions ((1 mark))
  •  These defects reduce blood flow from the left side of the heart to the rest of the body
  • (systemic circulation). Examples include
  •  Hypoplastic left heart syndrome: Underdevelopment of the left side of the heart
  • reducing blood flow to the body.
  •  Interrupted aortic arch: Incomplete development of the aorta, obstructing blood
  • flow to the body.
  • History ((1 mark))
  •  Assess duration, frequency, stool consistency, blood or mucus, vomiting, fever, and
  • abdominal pain.
  •  Record fluid intake, urine output, dietary history, antibiotic use, travel
  • contaminated food/water exposure, weight loss, and previous episodes.
  • Cups
  •  Cut-out cups prevent backward head tilting, while small-diameter and handled cups
  • improve grip and control.
  •  Spouted cups may help during bottle transition, while spout-free lids reduce spills
  • control liquid flow, and encourage lip closure.
  • Growth Impairment
  •  Inadequate energy, protein and essential nutrients reduce IGF-1 production and slow
  • normal growth, resulting in poor weight gain and reduced growth velocity.
  •  If undernutrition persists, it may lead to growth faltering, stunting and failure to
  • thrive.
  • Blood Glucose Tests
  •  Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥126 mg/dL after at least 8 hours of fasting.
  •  Random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL in the presence of classic symptoms, or 2
  • hour plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).
  •  HbA1c ≥6.5% indicates diabetes.
  • Hydrogen Breath Test (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  It is the most commonly used and reliable test for diagnosing lactose intolerance.
  •  The individual drinks a lactose-containing solution, and hydrogen and methane
  • levels in the exhaled breath are measured at regular intervals.
  •  Undigested lactose passes into the large intestine, where intestinal bacteria ferment
  • it and produce hydrogen and methane gases.
  •  Elevated hydrogen or methane levels in the breath indicate lactose malabsorption
  • and support the diagnosis of lactose intolerance.
  • Individualized Elimination Diet ((2 marks))
  •  Elimination diets are the cornerstone of dietary management of confirmed food
  • allergies and should be individualized according to the type and severity of allergy
  • number of allergens, age, nutritional status and affordability of alternatives.
  •  A single-food elimination diet removes only the confirmed offending food while
  • retaining other tolerated foods, helping maintain dietary variety and reduce
  • nutritional risks.
  •  A multiple-food elimination diet removes two or more confirmed allergens
  • requiring monitoring for inadequate energy, protein and micronutrient intake
  • feeding difficulties and growth faltering.
  •  Extensive or few-food elimination diets are reserved for selected diagnostic or
  • severe non-IgE-mediated conditions under specialist supervision because of their
  • nutritional and psychosocial risks.
  • Complementary Feeding
  •  Introduce age-appropriate fruits, vegetables, iron-rich foods, cereals and other
  • tolerated foods with suitable texture progression, avoiding unnecessary food
  • restrictions.
  • Sodium (Na⁺)
  •  Maintains extracellular fluid balance, nerve conduction, normal growth and
  • development.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Usually provided after the first few days of life to replace
  • losses; approximately 2–3 mEq/kg/day, individualized according to serum sodium
  • hydration and renal function.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 2–3 mEq/kg/day; very low birth weight (VLBW)
  • infants with increased renal losses or hyponatremia may require 4–8 mEq/kg/day or
  • more under medical supervision.
  • IAP Standards ((1 Mark))
  •  The Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP) growth charts are used to assess the
  • growth and nutritional status of children in India.
  •  Used for children aged 5-18 years.
  • Steps in interpretation ((1 mark))
  •  Measure the child's age, sex, weight, height and BMI.
  •  Plot the measurements on the appropriate growth chart.
  •  Compare the values with percentile curves or Z-scores.
  •  Interpret the child's nutritional status based on the position on the chart.
  • Interpretation of anthropometric parameters ((2 marks))
  •  Height-for-age: Below the 3rd percentile indicates short stature or stunting; between
  • the 3rd and 97th percentiles is generally considered normal.
  •  Weight-for-age: Below the 3rd percentile indicates underweight; between the 3rd
  • and 97th percentiles is generally considered normal.
  •  BMI-for-age (5–18 years): Used to classify thinness, normal weight, overweight
  • and obesity. The revised IAP charts use adult-equivalent BMI cut-offs of 23 kg/m²
  • for overweight and 27 kg/m² for obesity.
  •  Weight-for-height (under 5 years): Based on WHO standards; below −2 SD
  • indicates wasting and below −3 SD indicates severe wasting, while above +2 SD
  • indicates overweight.
  • Gluten-Free Diet ((1 mark))
  •  A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the only effective treatment for celiac disease.
  •  Completely avoid wheat, barley and rye to prevent intestinal damage and promote
  • healing of the intestinal mucosa.
  •  A balanced gluten-free diet helps restore nutrient absorption and supports normal
  • growth and development.

questions.question: Identify the major factors associated with nutritional deficiencies in / children with CP. a). Increased physical activity b). Increased food variety c). Increased nutritional requirement d). Poor oral-motor coordination, swallowing dysfunction, and GER
questions.solution_html:
• d) Poor oral-motor coordination, swallowing dysfunction, and GER
  • Weight ((1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  Body weight is one of the simplest and most widely used anthropometric
  • measurements for assessing nutritional status.
  •  Weight is measured using suitable weighing scales, such as Salter scales, beam
  • balance scales, or digital scales.
  •  The child should be weighed with minimal clothing, without shoes, and without
  • holding any support.
  •  For infants who cannot be weighed separately, the caregiver can be weighed while
  • holding the infant, and the caregiver’s weight is subtracted to obtain the infant’s
  • weight.
  • Right Heart Obstructive Lesions ((2 mark))
  •  These defects reduce blood flow from the heart to the lungs (pulmonary circulation)
  • affecting oxygenation of blood. Examples include
  •  Tetralogy of Fallot: Four heart abnormalities that reduce blood flow to the lungs
  • and cause cyanosis.
  •  Ebstein anomaly: Abnormal tricuspid valve development affecting blood flow
  • through the right side of the heart.
  •  Pulmonary atresia: Failure of the pulmonary valve to develop properly, blocking
  • blood flow to the lungs.
  •  Tricuspid atresia: Absence or abnormal development of the tricuspid valve
  • restricting blood flow through the right heart.
  • Physical Examination ((1 mark))
  •  Assess general appearance, consciousness, and hydration status.
  •  Check skin turgor, sunken eyes, dry mouth, thirst, pulse, circulation, and urine
  • output.
  •  Assess weight, growth pattern, and nutritional status.
  • Straws
  •  Improve sucking skills, lip strength, and oral control while promoting proper
  • drinking posture.
  •  Colourful or fun straws encourage children to practise drinking.
  • Weakened Immune System
  •  Undernutrition impairs innate and adaptive immunity, increasing susceptibility to
  • infections such as diarrhoea and respiratory infections.
  •  Infections reduce appetite and increase nutrient requirements, further worsening
  • undernutrition and creating an infection–undernutrition cycle.
  • Autoantibody Testing
  •  Autoantibodies help confirm autoimmune T1DM.
  •  Common antibodies include GAD65, IA-2, insulin autoantibody (IAA), ZnT8 and
  • islet cell antibody (ICA).
  • Blood Glucose Test (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  This test may be used when the hydrogen breath test does not provide clear results.
  •  Blood glucose levels are measured before and after the individual consumes a
  • lactose-containing solution.
  •  Normally, lactase breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose, resulting in an
  • increase in blood glucose levels.
  •  Little or no rise in blood glucose indicates inadequate lactose digestion and
  • absorption, supporting the diagnosis of lactose intolerance.
  • Specialized Diets for Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE) ((2 marks))
  •  One-food elimination diet (1FED): Usually eliminates cow's milk, allowing greater
  • dietary variety and better adherence.
  •  Two-food elimination diet (2FED): Commonly eliminates cow's milk and wheat.
  •  Four-food elimination diet (4FED): Commonly eliminates dairy, soy, egg and
  • wheat; it may be followed for approximately 8–12 weeks before reassessment and
  • supervised food reintroduction.
  •  More extensive elimination diets: Six-food or broader diets may be used in selected
  • cases, but increase nutritional risks and make adherence difficult.
  •  Elemental diet: Uses an amino-acid-based formula as the primary nutritional source
  • and is reserved for selected cases under specialist medical and dietetic supervision.
  • Food Label Reading
  •  Educate parents and children to read ingredient lists, identify hidden allergens and
  • alternative names, and understand precautionary statements such as “may contain.”
  • Potassium (K⁺)
  •  Maintains intracellular fluid balance, neuromuscular function and normal cardiac
  • activity.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Approximately 2–3 mEq/kg/day; introduced only after
  • adequate urine output and renal function are established to prevent hyperkalemia.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 2–3 mEq/kg/day, supplied through human milk or
  • preterm formula.
  • Gomez Classification ((1 Mark))
  •  Gomez classification is an early method used to assess protein-energy malnutrition
  • based on the percentage of expected weight-for-age.
  •  Weight for age (%) = (Actual weight of the child/ Median weight for age) x 100
  • Classification ((1 Mark))
  •  Normal: Above 90% of the expected weight.
  •  Mild malnutrition (Grade I): 76–90%.
  •  Moderate malnutrition (Grade II): 61–75%.
  •  Severe malnutrition (Grade III): Below 60%.
  • Limitations ((1 Mark))
  •  It does not consider height and cannot distinguish wasting from stunting.
  •  It does not assess overweight or obesity.
  • Common Nutritional Deficiencies ((2 marks))
  •  Iron: Deficiency may lead to anaemia.
  •  Calcium and vitamin D: Deficiency impairs bone mineralization and increases the
  • risk of osteopenia and osteoporosis.
  •  Folate and vitamin B12: Deficiency affects red blood cell formation and
  • neurological function.
  •  Zinc and magnesium: Deficiency may impair growth, wound healing and normal
  • body functions.
  •  Fibre: Low intake may contribute to constipation and poor gut health.
questions.final_answer: Option (d) Poor oral-motor coordination, swallowing dysfunction, and GER

questions.question: Identify the hormone-related pathway affected by undernutrition and / involved in normal growth. a). Growth hormone–IGF-1 axis b). Insulin-glucagon axis c). Antidiuretic hormone d). Thyroid-stimulating hormone axis
questions.solution_html:
• a) Growth hormone–IGF-1 axis
  • Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  MUAC indicates muscle development and helps identify wasting and protein
  • energy malnutrition.
  •  It is measured on the left upper arm using a flexible, non-stretchable tape.
  •  With the forearm bent at a right angle, mark the midpoint between the acromion
  • process and the tip of the ulna.
  •  Place the tape around the midpoint without compressing the tissues and record the
  • measurement to the nearest 0.1 cm.
  • Mixing Lesions ((1 mark))
  •  These defects allow oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood to mix, reducing the
  • oxygen supply delivered to the body. Examples include
  •  Transposition of the great arteries: The aorta and pulmonary artery arise from the
  • wrong ventricles, causing abnormal circulation.
  •  Truncus arteriosus: A single major artery arises from the heart instead of separate
  • aorta and pulmonary artery.
  • Laboratory Investigations ((2 mark))
  •  Blood tests to assess dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, anaemia, inflammation
  • and nutritional status.
  •  Stool examination to identify pathogens and parasites, especially in bloody or
  • persistent diarrhoea.
  • Spoons
  •  Shallow spoons ease food removal, while rubber-coated or plastic spoons are gentle
  • on sensitive mouths.
  •  Built-up or bent handles improve grip and control; spoon cuffs or holders secure the
  • spoon for self-feeding.
  • Fatigue and Weakness
  •  Inadequate energy intake causes the body to use stored fat and, during prolonged
  • deficiency, muscle tissue for energy.
  •  Loss of energy reserves and muscle mass leads to fatigue, weakness, reduced
  • physical activity and poor physical capacity.
  • C-Peptide Measurement
  •  C-peptide indicates the body's endogenous insulin production.
  •  Low or absent C-peptide suggests reduced insulin secretion due to pancreatic beta
  • cell destruction.
  • Stool Acidity Test (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  This test is mainly used in infants and young children who may not be able to
  • perform the hydrogen breath test.
  •  A stool sample is collected and examined after the child consumes lactose.
  •  Undigested lactose is fermented by intestinal bacteria, producing lactic acid and
  • other organic acids.
  •  A low stool pH indicates increased acidity due to organic acid production and
  • supports the diagnosis of lactose malabsorption.
  • Essay
  • Dietary Management of Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome
  • (FPIES) ((2 marks))
  •  Identify and avoid confirmed trigger foods that cause gastrointestinal symptoms
  • particularly repetitive vomiting and diarrhoea.
  •  Provide safe alternative foods to maintain adequate energy and protein intake.
  •  Maintain dietary diversity and prevent unnecessary restriction of multiple foods.
  •  Monitor nutritional status and growth regularly to prevent nutritional deficiencies
  • and growth faltering.
  • Other dietary management approaches ((4 marks), ½ mark for each point)
  • Cross-Contact Prevention
  •  Prevent accidental allergen transfer by using clean utensils, surfaces and cooking
  • equipment, and educating children, caregivers and teachers about allergen
  • avoidance.
  • Chloride (Cl⁻)
  •  Maintains acid–base balance, osmotic pressure and fluid regulation.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Added with sodium and potassium after the initial days
  • of life to maintain electrolyte and acid–base balance; requirements are
  • individualized.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Usually supplied along with sodium and potassium through
  • human milk or fortified human milk and preterm formula.
  • NCHS Standards ((1 Mark))
  •  The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) assess the growth and nutritional
  • status of children from birth to 18 years.
  • Steps in interpretation ((1 mark))
  •  Measure the child's age, sex, weight and height or length.
  •  Compare the measurements with NCHS reference values for children of the same
  • age and sex.
  •  Assess nutritional status using weight-for-age, height-for-age, weight-for-height
  • and BMI-for-age indices.
  • Interpretation of anthropometric indices ((1 Mark))
  •  Weight-for-age: Assesses underweight.
  •  Height-for-age: Identifies stunting or chronic malnutrition.
  •  Weight-for-height: Identifies wasting or acute malnutrition and can indicate
  • overweight.
  •  BMI-for-age: Helps assess thinness, overweight and obesity.
  • Nutrient Requirements ((2 marks))
  •  Correct nutritional deficiencies and restore normal nutrient absorption.
  •  Promote intestinal healing, healthy growth and development, and improved bone
  • and immune health.
  •  Prevent long-term complications such as anaemia and osteoporosis and improve
  • overall quality of life.
  •  Energy and protein: Adequate intake supports catch-up growth, tissue repair and
  • normal development.
  •  Iron: Include iron-rich foods to prevent and correct anaemia.
  •  Calcium and vitamin D: Ensure adequate intake for bone growth and mineralization.
  •  Folate, vitamin B12, zinc and magnesium: Provide adequate amounts to support
  • blood formation, immunity and growth.
  •  Dietary fibre: Include fibre-rich gluten-free foods to maintain bowel health and
  • prevent constipation.

questions.question: Identify the major urinary abnormality characteristic of nephrotic / syndrome a). Hematuria b). Heavy proteinuria c). Glycosuria d). Ketonuria
questions.solution_html:
• b) Heavy proteinuria
  • Head Circumference (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  Head circumference indicates head and brain growth, especially in children up to 3
  • years.
  •  It is measured using a narrow, non-stretchable measuring tape.
  •  Pass the tape above the eyebrows, around the sides of the head, and over the most
  • prominent part of the occiput.
  •  Adjust the tape to obtain the maximum circumference, pressing the hair against the
  • skull, and record the measurement accurately.
  • Other Investigations in Chronic Diarrhoea ((1 mark), any 2 points ½ mark each)
  •  Endoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy to identify intestinal abnormalities.
  •  Lactose hydrogen breath test to detect lactose malabsorption.
  •  Imaging when indicated to investigate underlying gastrointestinal conditions.
  • Plates and Bowls
  •  Plate guards and scoop dishes help children collect food easily.
  •  Suction-base dishes and non-slip mats prevent plates and bowls from sliding.
  • Weight Loss and Wasting
  •  Acute or severe undernutrition causes rapid weight loss and wasting, characterised
  • by low weight-for-height.
  •  Wasting indicates recent nutritional deprivation or illness and is associated with
  • impaired immunity, increased complications and mortality risk.
  • Ketone Testing
  •  Urine or blood ketone tests help identify ketone accumulation.
  •  These tests are important for detecting diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a serious
  • complication of T1DM.
  • Nutritional Substitution
  •  Follow the principle of “remove and replace” by providing safe alternatives that
  • maintain adequate energy, protein, calcium, vitamin D and other essential nutrients.
  • Calcium
  •  Essential for bone mineralization, skeletal growth, muscle contraction and nerve
  • function.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Approximately 500–600 mg/L, administered with
  • phosphorus; serum calcium and alkaline phosphatase levels are monitored.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 165–180 mg/100 kcal; fortified human milk or
  • preterm formula helps prevent osteopenia of prematurity.
  • Dietary Modifications ((5 marks))
  •  Include naturally gluten-free foods such as fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts, seeds
  • meat, poultry, fish, eggs and milk if tolerated.
  •  Replace gluten-containing grains with rice, millet, sorghum, quinoa, buckwheat and
  • amaranth; certified gluten-free oats may be included if uncontaminated and well
  • tolerated.
  •  Limit processed gluten-free foods because they may be high in fat, sugar and salt
  • but low in fibre and essential micronutrients.
  •  Read food labels carefully to identify hidden gluten sources such as wheat starch
  • and malt, and choose appropriately labelled gluten-free products.
  •  Prevent cross-contamination during storage, preparation and cooking by using
  • separate utensils, cutting boards, toasters and condiment containers when necessary.
  •  Check food preparation practices when eating outside the home and ensure
  • medications, vitamins and supplements are suitable for a gluten-free diet.
  •  Regularly monitor weight, height, growth patterns, dietary intake and adherence to
  • the gluten-free diet.
  •  Assess iron, calcium, vitamin D, folate, vitamin B12 and other nutrient levels when
  • clinically indicated.
  •  Provide vitamin or mineral supplementation when deficiencies are confirmed or
  • dietary intake is inadequate.
  •  Arrange regular follow-up with a paediatric gastroenterologist and registered
  • dietitian, and provide continuous nutrition education to children and caregivers.

questions.question: State the main purpose of the Specific Carbohydrate Diet. / a). To increase sucrose intake b). To increase grain consumption c). To restore and maintain a healthy gut microbial population d). To increase lactose intake
questions.solution_html:
• c) To restore and maintain a healthy gut microbial population
  • Skinfold Thickness (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  Skinfold thickness is used to estimate body fat and assess the child’s fat reserves.
  •  Common measurement sites include the triceps, subscapular, and suprailiac regions.
  •  The skin and underlying fat are gently pinched between the thumb and forefinger
  • without including muscle, and the fold is measured using a skinfold caliper.
  •  Three measurements are recommended, and their average is calculated for greater
  • accuracy.
  • Seating and Positioning
  •  Supportive chairs, footrests, trays, and cushions provide head, neck, and trunk
  • stability and improve hand-to-mouth coordination.
  •  Proper positioning improves feeding efficiency, reduces fatigue, and lowers choking
  • and aspiration risks.
  • Increased Susceptibility to Infection and Mortality
  •  Undernourished children have a higher risk of frequent infections, particularly
  • diarrhoeal and respiratory infections, due to impaired immunity and inadequate
  • body reserves.
  •  Severe undernutrition, especially wasting, increases the risk of serious
  • complications and death.
  • Additional Investigations
  •  Serum electrolytes are assessed to identify electrolyte imbalances.
  •  Renal function tests help evaluate kidney function, particularly during acute illness
  • or DKA.
  • Growth and Nutritional Monitoring
  •  Regularly monitor weight, height/length, BMI-for-age, dietary diversity and
  • nutrient adequacy, with supplementation or biochemical assessment when clinically
  • indicated.
  • Phosphorus
  •  Required for bone mineralization, ATP production, energy metabolism and normal
  • cellular function.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Approximately 400–500 mg/L, administered with
  • calcium; serum phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase levels are monitored.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 82–100 mg/100 kcal; adequate intake supports
  • bone growth and prevents metabolic bone disease.
questions.final_answer: Option (c) To restore and maintain a healthy gut microbial population

questions.question: State the purpose of early identification of ADHD. / a). To improve outcomes through early recognition and management b). To completely prevent ADHD c). To eliminate the need for treatment d). To avoid educational support
questions.solution_html:
• a) To improve outcomes through early recognition and management
  • Feeding Difficulties
  •  Address food refusal, fear of eating, limited food variety and texture difficulties
  • through positive feeding practices and appropriate feeding or psychological support.
  • Iron
  •  Essential for haemoglobin synthesis, red blood cell formation, oxygen transport and
  • neurodevelopment.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Not routinely provided; when indicated, approximately
  • 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/day may be used according to clinical requirements.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 2–4 mg/kg/day after two weeks of age; infants
  • receiving erythropoietin may require higher amounts, and breastfed preterm infants
  • generally require supplementation.
questions.final_answer: Option To improve outcomes through early recognition and management

questions.question: Identify the body fluids most commonly used for biochemical / assessment of nutritional status. a). Saliva and sweat b). Blood and urine c). Cerebrospinal fluid and saliva d). Lymph and sweat
questions.solution_html:
• b) Blood and urine
  • School and Social Activities
  •  Educate teachers, caregivers and food-service personnel about allergen avoidance
  • and emergency plans, enabling safe participation in school and social activities.
  • Zinc
  •  Supports growth, immune function, wound healing and enzyme activity.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Approximately 400 µg/kg/day, particularly important
  • during prolonged PN.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 1–3 mg/kg/day, usually supplied through fortified
  • human milk or preterm formula.

questions.solution_html:
• c) Type 2 diabetes mellitus
  • Education and Follow-up
  •  Educate families about allergen avoidance, symptom recognition, cross-contact

  • Vitamin A
  •  Essential for vision, epithelial integrity, immune function and lung development.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Provided through paediatric intravenous multivitamin
  • preparations. Recommendation: 700-1500 IU/Kg/day.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 1300–3300 IU/kg/day, generally supplied through
  • fortified human milk or preterm formula.

questions.question: A child is prescribed a classical ketogenic diet with a 4:1 ratio. Which / meal composition best represents this ratio? a). 4 g carbohydrate : 1 g fat b). 4 g fat : 1 g protein + carbohydrate c). 4 g protein : 1 g fat d). 4 g fat : 1 g protein
questions.solution_html:
• b) 4 g fat: 1 g protein + carbohydrate
  • Vitamin D
  •  Promotes calcium absorption, bone mineralization and prevention of metabolic
  • bone disease.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Provided through paediatric intravenous multivitamin
  • preparations.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 400-700 IU/day according to the supplied
  • material; requirements should be individualized based on current neonatal guidance
  • and total intake.
questions.final_answer: Option (b) 4 g fat: 1 g protein + carbohydrate

questions.question: Name the metabolic complication involving abnormal acid-base balance / in CKD. a). Metabolic acidosis b). Respiratory alkalosis c). Metabolic alkalosis d). Respiratory acidosis
questions.solution_html:
• a) Metabolic acidosis
  • Short Answer
  • Vitamin E
  •  Acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage and helping prevent
  • haemolytic anaemia.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Included in paediatric intravenous multivitamin
  • preparations.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 6–12 IU/kg/day; pharmacological doses are
  • avoided because of possible adverse effects.

questions.question: Describe the clinical manifestation of iodine deficiency
questions.solution_html:
•  Goitre: Enlargement of the thyroid gland located at the front of the neck.
  •  Other manifestations: Cretinism (physical and mental retardation) and deaf
  • mutism (hearing and speech impairment).
  • Vitamin K
  •  Essential for blood coagulation and prevention of haemorrhagic disease of the
  • newborn.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Vitamin K prophylaxis is given intramuscularly at birth
  • commonly 0.5–1 mg as specified in the supplied material; subsequent provision
  • may occur through intravenous multivitamin preparations.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Routine prophylaxis is given at birth; subsequent intake is

questions.question: Identify the component of the TICLS framework which assesses a / child’s muscle tone and spontaneous movement? a). Tone b). Interactiveness c). Look/Gaze d). Speech/Cry
questions.solution_html:
• a) Tone
  • Height/Length (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  Length is measured in children below 2 years using an infantometer, with the child
  • lying down (known as recumbent or crown-heel length).
  •  The child’s head is placed against the fixed headpiece, the body is kept straight, and
  • the knees and ankles are gently pressed flat against the board.
  •  Standing height (stature) is measured in children aged 2 years and above using a
  • stadiometer or wall-mounted measuring board, with bare feet and the child standing
  • erect.
  •  The head is positioned horizontally, and the measurement is recorded to the nearest
  • 0.1 cm.
  • Left Heart Obstructive Lesions ((1 mark))
  •  These defects reduce blood flow from the left side of the heart to the rest of the body
  • (systemic circulation). Examples include
  •  Hypoplastic left heart syndrome: Underdevelopment of the left side of the heart
  • reducing blood flow to the body.
  •  Interrupted aortic arch: Incomplete development of the aorta, obstructing blood
  • flow to the body.
  • History ((1 mark))
  •  Assess duration, frequency, stool consistency, blood or mucus, vomiting, fever, and
  • abdominal pain.
  •  Record fluid intake, urine output, dietary history, antibiotic use, travel
  • contaminated food/water exposure, weight loss, and previous episodes.
  • Cups
  •  Cut-out cups prevent backward head tilting, while small-diameter and handled cups
  • improve grip and control.
  •  Spouted cups may help during bottle transition, while spout-free lids reduce spills
  • control liquid flow, and encourage lip closure.
  • Growth Impairment
  •  Inadequate energy, protein and essential nutrients reduce IGF-1 production and slow
  • normal growth, resulting in poor weight gain and reduced growth velocity.
  •  If undernutrition persists, it may lead to growth faltering, stunting and failure to
  • thrive.
  • Blood Glucose Tests
  •  Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥126 mg/dL after at least 8 hours of fasting.
  •  Random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL in the presence of classic symptoms, or 2
  • hour plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).
  •  HbA1c ≥6.5% indicates diabetes.
  • Hydrogen Breath Test (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  It is the most commonly used and reliable test for diagnosing lactose intolerance.
  •  The individual drinks a lactose-containing solution, and hydrogen and methane
  • levels in the exhaled breath are measured at regular intervals.
  •  Undigested lactose passes into the large intestine, where intestinal bacteria ferment
  • it and produce hydrogen and methane gases.
  •  Elevated hydrogen or methane levels in the breath indicate lactose malabsorption
  • and support the diagnosis of lactose intolerance.
  • Individualized Elimination Diet ((2 marks))
  •  Elimination diets are the cornerstone of dietary management of confirmed food
  • allergies and should be individualized according to the type and severity of allergy
  • number of allergens, age, nutritional status and affordability of alternatives.
  •  A single-food elimination diet removes only the confirmed offending food while
  • retaining other tolerated foods, helping maintain dietary variety and reduce
  • nutritional risks.
  •  A multiple-food elimination diet removes two or more confirmed allergens
  • requiring monitoring for inadequate energy, protein and micronutrient intake
  • feeding difficulties and growth faltering.
  •  Extensive or few-food elimination diets are reserved for selected diagnostic or
  • severe non-IgE-mediated conditions under specialist supervision because of their
  • nutritional and psychosocial risks.
  • Complementary Feeding
  •  Introduce age-appropriate fruits, vegetables, iron-rich foods, cereals and other
  • tolerated foods with suitable texture progression, avoiding unnecessary food
  • restrictions.
  • Sodium (Na⁺)
  •  Maintains extracellular fluid balance, nerve conduction, normal growth and
  • development.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Usually provided after the first few days of life to replace
  • losses; approximately 2–3 mEq/kg/day, individualized according to serum sodium
  • hydration and renal function.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 2–3 mEq/kg/day; very low birth weight (VLBW)
  • infants with increased renal losses or hyponatremia may require 4–8 mEq/kg/day or
  • more under medical supervision.
  • IAP Standards ((1 Mark))
  •  The Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP) growth charts are used to assess the
  • growth and nutritional status of children in India.
  •  Used for children aged 5-18 years.
  • Steps in interpretation ((1 mark))
  •  Measure the child's age, sex, weight, height and BMI.
  •  Plot the measurements on the appropriate growth chart.
  •  Compare the values with percentile curves or Z-scores.
  •  Interpret the child's nutritional status based on the position on the chart.
  • Interpretation of anthropometric parameters ((2 marks))
  •  Height-for-age: Below the 3rd percentile indicates short stature or stunting; between
  • the 3rd and 97th percentiles is generally considered normal.
  •  Weight-for-age: Below the 3rd percentile indicates underweight; between the 3rd
  • and 97th percentiles is generally considered normal.
  •  BMI-for-age (5–18 years): Used to classify thinness, normal weight, overweight
  • and obesity. The revised IAP charts use adult-equivalent BMI cut-offs of 23 kg/m²
  • for overweight and 27 kg/m² for obesity.
  •  Weight-for-height (under 5 years): Based on WHO standards; below −2 SD
  • indicates wasting and below −3 SD indicates severe wasting, while above +2 SD
  • indicates overweight.
  • Gluten-Free Diet ((1 mark))
  •  A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the only effective treatment for celiac disease.
  •  Completely avoid wheat, barley and rye to prevent intestinal damage and promote
  • healing of the intestinal mucosa.
  •  A balanced gluten-free diet helps restore nutrient absorption and supports normal
  • growth and development.

questions.question: Identify the major factors associated with nutritional deficiencies in / children with CP. a). Increased physical activity b). Increased food variety c). Increased nutritional requirement d). Poor oral-motor coordination, swallowing dysfunction, and GER

• d) Poor oral-motor coordination, swallowing dysfunction, and GER
  • Weight ((1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  Body weight is one of the simplest and most widely used anthropometric
  • measurements for assessing nutritional status.
  •  Weight is measured using suitable weighing scales, such as Salter scales, beam
  • balance scales, or digital scales.
  •  The child should be weighed with minimal clothing, without shoes, and without
  • holding any support.
  •  For infants who cannot be weighed separately, the caregiver can be weighed while
  • holding the infant, and the caregiver’s weight is subtracted to obtain the infant’s
  • weight.
  • Right Heart Obstructive Lesions ((2 mark))
  •  These defects reduce blood flow from the heart to the lungs (pulmonary circulation)
  • affecting oxygenation of blood. Examples include
  •  Tetralogy of Fallot: Four heart abnormalities that reduce blood flow to the lungs
  • and cause cyanosis.
  •  Ebstein anomaly: Abnormal tricuspid valve development affecting blood flow
  • through the right side of the heart.
  •  Pulmonary atresia: Failure of the pulmonary valve to develop properly, blocking
  • blood flow to the lungs.
  •  Tricuspid atresia: Absence or abnormal development of the tricuspid valve
  • restricting blood flow through the right heart.
  • Physical Examination ((1 mark))
  •  Assess general appearance, consciousness, and hydration status.
  •  Check skin turgor, sunken eyes, dry mouth, thirst, pulse, circulation, and urine
  • output.
  •  Assess weight, growth pattern, and nutritional status.
  • Straws
  •  Improve sucking skills, lip strength, and oral control while promoting proper
  • drinking posture.
  •  Colourful or fun straws encourage children to practise drinking.
  • Weakened Immune System
  •  Undernutrition impairs innate and adaptive immunity, increasing susceptibility to
  • infections such as diarrhoea and respiratory infections.
  •  Infections reduce appetite and increase nutrient requirements, further worsening
  • undernutrition and creating an infection–undernutrition cycle.
  • Autoantibody Testing
  •  Autoantibodies help confirm autoimmune T1DM.
  •  Common antibodies include GAD65, IA-2, insulin autoantibody (IAA), ZnT8 and
  • islet cell antibody (ICA).
  • Blood Glucose Test (1/(2 mark) for each point)
  •  This test may be used when the hydrogen breath test does not provide clear results.
  •  Blood glucose levels are measured before and after the individual consumes a
  • lactose-containing solution.
  •  Normally, lactase breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose, resulting in an
  • increase in blood glucose levels.
  •  Little or no rise in blood glucose indicates inadequate lactose digestion and
  • absorption, supporting the diagnosis of lactose intolerance.
  • Specialized Diets for Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE) ((2 marks))
  •  One-food elimination diet (1FED): Usually eliminates cow's milk, allowing greater
  • dietary variety and better adherence.
  •  Two-food elimination diet (2FED): Commonly eliminates cow's milk and wheat.
  •  Four-food elimination diet (4FED): Commonly eliminates dairy, soy, egg and
  • wheat; it may be followed for approximately 8–12 weeks before reassessment and
  • supervised food reintroduction.
  •  More extensive elimination diets: Six-food or broader diets may be used in selected
  • cases, but increase nutritional risks and make adherence difficult.
  •  Elemental diet: Uses an amino-acid-based formula as the primary nutritional source
  • and is reserved for selected cases under specialist medical and dietetic supervision.
  • Food Label Reading
  •  Educate parents and children to read ingredient lists, identify hidden allergens and
  • alternative names, and understand precautionary statements such as “may contain.”
  • Potassium (K⁺)
  •  Maintains intracellular fluid balance, neuromuscular function and normal cardiac
  • activity.
  •  Parenteral nutrition (PN): Approximately 2–3 mEq/kg/day; introduced only after
  • adequate urine output and renal function are established to prevent hyperkalemia.
  •  Enteral nutrition: Approximately 2–3 mEq/kg/day, supplied through human milk or
  • preterm formula.
  • Gomez Classification ((1 Mark))
  •  Gomez classification is an early method used to assess protein-energy malnutrition
  • based on the percentage of expected weight-for-age.
  •  Weight for age (%) = (Actual weight of the child/ Median weight for age) x 100
  • Classification ((1 Mark))
  •  Normal: Above 90% of the expected weight.
  •  Mild malnutrition (Grade I): 76–90%.
  •  Moderate malnutrition (Grade II): 61–75%.
  •  Severe malnutrition (Grade III): Below 60%.
  • Limitations ((1 Mark))
  •  It does not consider height and cannot distinguish wasting from stunting.
  •  It does not assess overweight or obesity.
  • Common Nutritional Deficiencies ((2 marks))
  •  Iron: Deficiency may lead to anaemia.
  •  Calcium and vitamin D: Deficiency impairs bone mineralization and increases the
  • risk of osteopenia and osteoporosis.
  •  Folate and vitamin B12: Deficiency affects red blood cell formation and
  • neurological function.
  •  Zinc and magnesium: Deficiency may impair growth, wound healing and normal
  • body functions.
  •  Fibre: Low intake may contribute to constipation and poor gut health.

  •  The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) assess the growth and nutritional

  • Steps in interpretation ((1 mark))
